tagline: Mahé, Praslin and La Digue — an Indian Ocean luxury triangle that lives on the inter-island ferry.
summary: The Seychelles Inner Islands are a compact granitic cluster — Mahé with the capital Victoria and the international gateway, Praslin with the Vallée de Mai, and La Digue with its famous beaches — linked today by fast catamaran ferries and small inter-island flights. It is one of the world's highest-end beach destinations, and almost every guest journey includes a water transfer. A clean, stabilised foiling tier is the natural premium layer over the existing ferry triangle.
why_marine_mobility: The Seychelles story is the inter-island transfer. Mahé's airport feeds Praslin and La Digue by catamaran ferry and light aircraft; the short, busy Praslin–La Digue hop is one of the most travelled tourist legs in the Indian Ocean. The ferries are good but conventional, weather-exposed and fixed-schedule, and the high-end resort clientele has no on-demand premium water option. Navier's Pioneer II foiling tier flies the whole Inner-Islands triangle smooth, dry and clean today, while the Quanta-LR hybrid range reaches the scattered Outer Islands that ferries cannot practically serve.

demand_signals.label: High-end resort dependency
demand_signals.note: Seychelles is a premier luxury beach destination (Six Senses Zil Pasyon, Constance Lémuria, Four Seasons, North Island); nearly every guest journey includes an inter-island water or air transfer — a captive, high-value, recurring market.

demand_signals.label: The Mahé–Praslin–La Digue triangle
demand_signals.note: The Inner-Islands ferry triangle is one of the Indian Ocean's busiest tourist water corridors, with frequent daily catamaran sailings between the three main islands.

demand_signals.label: Inter-island necessity
demand_signals.note: Praslin and La Digue residents and workers depend on the ferry links for daily transport, supply and healthcare access — core connective infrastructure, not just tourism.

use_cases.body: Praslin to La Digue: the short, heavily-travelled tourist hop flown smooth and dry on Pioneer II — a quiet, on-demand premium alternative to the conventional catamaran shuttle.
Mahé (Victoria) to Praslin: the core Inner-Islands transfer linking the gateway island to the resorts of Praslin and the Vallée de Mai — clean, all-hours and matched to a high-end clientele.

Mahé to the Outer Islands: long-range Quanta-LR trunks to scattered private-island resorts (Desroches, Alphonse, the Amirantes) that today depend on costly light aircraft and push beyond practical ferry range.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire Inner-Islands triangle — Mahé to Praslin, Praslin to La Digue, and the Sainte Anne Marine Park hops off Victoria — sits well inside Pioneer II's 70-nautical-mile range at 30 knots, commercial-ready today and a clean premium upgrade on the catamaran ferry.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The Outer Islands (Desroches, Alphonse, the Amirantes, ~120–200+ nm from Mahé) are Quanta-LR corridors (~700 nm hybrid range, H2 2026+), reaching private-island resorts that today rely on expensive light aircraft, with diesel refuel removing the charging-infrastructure dependence on remote atolls.

Mahé (Victoria) ↔ Praslin — the core gateway transfer
Mahé (Victoria) ↔ Cerf Island (Sainte Anne Marine Park)

transit_planning: For a resort group, a ferry operator or the tourism authority: start with the proven Inner-Islands triangle on Pioneer II — a clean, all-hours premium tier over the existing catamaran service, riding the existing jetties at Victoria, Praslin and La Digue — then add the long Outer-Islands trunks on Quanta-LR as range comes online, opening private-island resorts that today depend on light aircraft. No new shoreside infrastructure is required.
competitive_landscape: Inter-island travel today runs on fast catamaran ferries (reliable but conventional, fixed-schedule and weather-exposed) and small inter-island flights (fast but costly, weight- and weather-limited). There is no clean, on-demand premium water tier. Navier's foiling craft is the missing premium-but-practical option: smoother and quieter than the catamaran, cheaper and less weather-bound than a light aircraft, and clean — matched to a luxury market with no comparable water product today.
regulatory_note: Maritime transport is overseen by the Seychelles Maritime Safety Authority (SMSA) and the Seychelles Ports Authority; passenger operation requires vessel certification and route licensing. Inner-Islands marine-park areas (Sainte Anne, Curieuse) are managed by the Seychelles National Parks Authority — a natural early touchpoint for protected-water routes.
seasonality: Seychelles is a year-round destination near the equator, but the southeast trade winds (roughly May–Sep) bring stronger winds and choppier seas — especially on exposed crossings — while the northwest monsoon (Nov–Mar) is calmer and more humid. A stabilised foiling craft holds comfort and schedule through the windier trade-wind months when conventional ferries are roughest.
